title: Recommended to His Successors
aliases: The Cargo Is Still Out There
logline: A half-kilometre of open grass between a city and the sea, cleared before a fort, raced on for most of a century and walked on ever since, carries at its sea edge a stone that says what the walk was for. The texts being taught say that the same act is wanting or not according to its aim, and that the aim does not show; the film watches one lawn for one whole day, from empty to full, from a single fixed height, and never says what anyone on it wants.
human_question: If the same walk by the sea can be taken for health, for pleasure, to be seen or to keep the dust off my clothes, and nothing about the walk is different, where exactly is the difference?

place.what_kind_of_place: A long, flat, treeless seafront lawn in the middle of a capital, about half a kilometre of grass between the sea wall and a line of roads and towers, with an old colonial hotel closing its far end. It was kept open in front of a fort, used as a racecourse until the 1890s, given a paved promenade along the sea wall in the 1850s, and is now the city's largest open public space. At the sea edge of the promenade stands a small stone post carrying an inscription about who the walk was meant for.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Because it changes completely every day and does it in the open. Before dawn it is an empty green plane with white surf breaking against the wall and the hotel lit at the far end; through the morning it is walkers and runners on a bare lawn in hard light; by late afternoon it fills, and at sunset it holds thousands of people, kites by the hundred over the grass, food-stall lights along the landward edge, and the sun going down into the open ocean on the lawn's seaward side. Seen from one high fixed point, the whole transformation is a single frame that fills and empties like a tide.
place.what_moves_or_changes: The crowd, the light and the sea, and nothing else. The sun crosses from behind the city to the sea horizon; the surf rises and falls against the wall; kites go up with the afternoon sea breeze and come down at dark; the lawn's own colour runs from grey-blue to green to gold to black under street light. The ground, the wall and the stone do not change at all, which is the film's argument.
place.when_it_looks_best: A clear dry-season weekend day, when the evening crowd is largest and the sun sets into a clean horizon; the south-west monsoon months give heavier surf over the wall but more cloud and rain. The whole film is one day, from about 05:00 to about 19:30, shot on a single date.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A day in the life of one open lawn by the sea, told as a single locked time-lapse from a high vantage at its landward end looking down its length to the sea and the old hotel: empty at first light, walkers at seven, heat and emptiness at noon, the crowd arriving through the afternoon, kites filling the air, and the sun going into the ocean over thousands of people. Cut into it, in real time and at ground level, a small stone post at the sea wall, first in blue pre-dawn light and last under a street lamp at night. The payoff is not a cut but a change of speed: at the moment the sun touches the sea the time-lapse slows and drops into real time, and the full lawn is held, live, with its sound, for as long as the light lasts. The film is a sunset and a crowd, and works entirely without words.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The voice gives the lawn's written history as a history of stated aims: a governor's stone that says the walk was built for the ladies and children of the town; a newspaper editor's reason that the red dust of the old ground spoiled boots and clothes; a French traveller who came at dawn and dusk and saw neither ladies nor children, and called the cleared ground a pretext for turf; a racing club that left because it could not fence the ground or keep the traffic off it; a gambling crisis written down by a journalist in 1872. Against that it sets the texts' list of the ordinary occasions of wanting, sport and watching sport, pleasure trips, fine things prepared and shown, and their rule that the same acts are not unwholesome when done with usefulness or kindness in front. The high fixed frame is the honest position for this argument: from it every person is a moving point, nobody's face can be read, and the voice can say, truthfully, that nothing in the frame shows why anyone is there. The one place the aim was ever written down, the stone, turns out to survive in two versions.

sequence.on_screen: Pre-dawn, blue light, ground level at the sea wall. A small square stone post, waist high, with surf breaking white behind it. The lens moves in real time across the carved lines, left to right, never lingering on the first line (the walk's name), and stops on the words about ladies and children.
sequence.voice: In 1864 a French traveller copied the words cut on a grey stone post at the edge of this lawn. The walk along the sea, it said, was begun by the governor, Sir Henry Ward, in 1856, completed in 1859, and 'recommended to his successors, in the interest of the ladies and children' of the city. It is one of the few places where the reason for a thing is written on the thing.

sequence.on_screen: The high fixed frame, from above the landward end of the lawn looking down its whole length: grey-green grass, the promenade along the sea wall, surf, the old hotel lit at the far end, the sea horizon. The time-lapse begins; the first walkers appear as moving points on the promenade.
sequence.voice: A stone can state an aim. It cannot show one. The texts taught in this series draw their line exactly there. They list the ordinary occasions of wanting: sport and watching sport, fine clothes, fine things looked at for the pleasure of it, a trip taken for enjoyment. Then they say the same acts are not unwholesome when faith, kindness or compassion, or a clear sense of what is useful, is put in front of them. Food cooked to quiet hunger. Clothes made to keep off cold and heat and insects. The act can be identical. What differs is why.

sequence.on_screen: Time-lapse, early morning: runners and walkers streak along the promenade in both directions, a few groups on the grass, long shadows from the city side pointing at the sea. The lawn is still mostly empty.
sequence.voice: The record gives this walk more than one reason. A newspaper editor of the town, writing of those years, said that before it was built a stroll on the sea side was next to impossible for ladies, because the red dust of the old ground got onto boots and clothing. A later writer, remembering 1861, called the lawn the place where the whole of society came of an afternoon to eat the air. The French traveller came at the only hours, he said, when the walk could be used without punishment, early and just before sunset, and saw neither ladies nor children there.

sequence.on_screen: Time-lapse, midday: the lawn nearly empty under a white sky, heat shimmer over the grass, the surf the only fast thing in the frame. A few points cross it and are gone.
sequence.voice: He thought the whole cleared ground was a mistake. The English, he wrote, had stripped a vast space south of the fort under the pretext of green lawns and a racecourse, carrying their own latitude into the tropics out of a passion for turf. For most of that century this lawn was also where the town's horses were raced. The texts put gambling, sport and watching sport on their list without any exemption, and the film does not look for one.

sequence.on_screen: Time-lapse, afternoon: the crowd begins to arrive from the landward side and spread across the grass; the first kites go up with the sea breeze; stalls light up along the far edge. Nobody in the frame is larger than a point.
sequence.voice: A history of the island printed in 1907 keeps two things from the racing years apart. One is ordinary: the club could never fence this ground or keep the traffic off it, and once a cart of beer barrels was run into by the field in the middle of a race, so in 1893 the racing moved to a course that could be closed. The other, set down by a journalist who arrived in 1872, is a plan to hold one horse back in one race in order to win on another and take the betting public's money. The plan failed, he wrote, and the club broke up.

sequence.on_screen: Time-lapse, late afternoon into sunset: the lawn full from wall to road, hundreds of kites against a gold sky, the sun dropping towards the sea at the right of the frame. As the sun touches the horizon the time-lapse slows, and slows, and drops into real time: the full lawn, live, with its own sound of sea and voices, held without a cut.
sequence.voice: The texts weigh wanting that goes as far as taking what is not given as strong, and ordinary fondness for one's own as weak. They weigh wanting that comes with a story excusing it as heavier than wanting without one, and the flat, unexcited kind as heavier than the glad kind. None of these weights can be seen from here. From this height nobody on the lawn is anything but a moving point, and the film does not say what anyone on it wants.

sequence.on_screen: Night, ground level again at the sea wall: the same stone post under a street lamp, the lit crowd soft and out of focus behind it, the surf audible. The lens holds on the words about ladies and children, then lets the frame go dark with the lamp still on.
sequence.voice: A handbook of 1882 copied this stone as saying the walk was for the use of the ladies and gentlemen. Every other copy says ladies and children. Even the one place where the aim was written down has come down in two versions. The texts never asked the stone. They ask each mind that walks past it, and only that mind can answer.

concept_merge.why_together: C005 supplies the question and C006 the scale on which the answer would be weighed. C005's Margaya lists the everyday occasions of greed-rooted minds, gambling, sport and watching sport, looking at beautiful things for enjoyment, preparing dear objects such as vehicles [C005-M:L5], courtship and pleasure trips [C005-M:L7], and then draws its line by aim, not act: the same earning, spending, dressing and eating are not unwholesome with faith, loving-kindness or compassion foremost, or with wisdom foremost 'considering usefulness' [C005-M:L9], as in food prepared to quiet hunger [C005-M:L13] and clothes made against cold, heat and insects [C005-M:L17]. This lawn's written record is a sequence of stated aims for one piece of ground, and the aims are exactly the kind the text sorts: a walk for others' benefit, a walk to keep dust off clothes, a lawn of turf for the pleasure of turf, racing and betting. C006 then says that a greed-rooted mind has three dials, joy or neutrality, a justifying view or none, prompted or unprompted [C006-M:L3–L17], and ranks them: the courses of action such as taking what is not given are strong, ordinary fondness for wife, children and wealth weak; view-joined outweighs view-free, unprompted outweighs prompted, neutral outweighs joyful [C006-M:L19]. The 1872 racing record puts one documented act of the heavy kind (a scheme to take the betting public's money) beside the ordinary pleasures of a race day, which is the distinction the Margaya makes.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the location cannot settle the question, and that its own documents already know it. C005 alone would make this a list of uses; C006 alone would make it a film about gamblers. Together they show that even the aims written down about the lawn are claims, sometimes contradicted by the next witness, and that the weights C006 assigns belong to single minds that no stone, no club minute and no camera can read. The high fixed frame is the treatment that follows from this: it keeps every person too small to judge, and gives the viewer a whole day of a place whose every visible act could have come from any of the eight greed-rooted kinds, or from none of them.

concept_links.why: The Margaya's line between greed-rooted and not is drawn by aim, not act [C005-M:L9] [C005-M:L11] [C005-M:L13] [C005-M:L15–L19], and its list of occasions names gambling, sport, watching sport, looking at beautiful things for enjoyment and preparing dear objects [C005-M:L5] and pleasure trips [C005-M:L7]. This lawn's record is one of the few places on the island where the aim of a public act was cut into the thing itself, and where the next witnesses gave different aims: the stone (for the ladies and children), a newspaper editor (to keep the red dust off boots and clothing), a French traveller of 1864 (a pretext for a passion for turf, used by neither ladies nor children), and a racing club that left because it could not close the ground. Exemption rulings, read from the source lines: the walk is undecidable, since spending with usefulness foremost [C005-M:L9] and protection of clothing [C005-M:L17] would exempt it, and a pleasure trip [C005-M:L7] would not, and no document can say which aim stood foremost in any walker or in the governor; racing and betting are not exempt, since M:L5 lists gambling, sport and watching sport with no qualifier; tonight's crowd is never ruled on at all. The film says 'not unwholesome' for the exempt branch and never 'wholesome', because the Margaya calls only the feeding of animals as a kindness wholesome outright [C005-M:L21], and the digest flags the rest for expert check. Three does_not_transfer lines bind it: 'art and sport are sinful' (the list is about the enjoying mind, so the film never calls racing, kites or play a fault); 'minimalism or self-denial is virtue' (the source allows good clothes against contempt, so the empty lawn is never presented as the pure state); and 'attachment to family is toxic' (the stone's ladies and children are never framed as objects of greed, and no family on the lawn is shown as wanting).

The Margaya's eight greed-rooted minds turn on joy or neutrality, a justifying view or none, and prompting or none, with prompting including one's own urging of a hesitating mind [C006-M:L3–L17] [C006-M:L5]; its ranking is that the courses of action such as taking what is not given are strong and fondness for family and wealth weak, view-joined stronger than view-free, unprompted stronger than prompted, and neutral stronger than joyful [C006-M:L19]. The 1872 racing record, as printed in 1907, sets a scheme to 'ramp the public' by holding one horse back in one race to win on another beside the ordinary pleasures of a race day, which is the strong-weak distinction as a document: an act aimed at taking the betting public's money against the enjoyment of watching. The film goes no further. It names nobody in the scheme (the source calls them only 'a few sparks'), says the plan failed as the source says, and does not assign any dial to anyone, because a plan is on record and a mind is not. Two does_not_transfer lines are used directly: 'calm means good' (the voice says the flat kind is weighed heavier, so a calm crowd is not presented as innocent), and 'guilt-free pleasure' (the texts' justifying story makes wanting heavier, which is why the French traveller's word 'pretext' is quoted as his accusation and not adopted). The line forbidding any mapping of wrong view onto a community's faith is kept: the only views in the film are the texts' own examples, never a belief of anyone on the lawn.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That the same act, a walk by the sea, a day at the races, a kite on a string, can be moved by quite different aims, and that the aim does not show: not from the ground, not from above, and not even from a stone that was carved to announce it. And that the texts being taught agree, and put the difference inside each single mind, where no camera and no inscription reaches.
what_must_be_real: The whole time-lapse is one real day from one fixed position, dawn to dark, on the date stated; it is never assembled from several days, and the slowdown into real time happens on the actual sunset of that day. Nobody is identifiable in the high frame; no face, family or child is picked out or followed; no vendor or stall is featured. The stone is filmed as it stands; if it is a later copy of the original, the film says so in the credits and never implies otherwise. No banner, protest material, political gathering or state ceremony appears; if one is on the lawn on the day, that day is abandoned. No quotation is spoken that has not been read in its printed source, and the two versions of the inscription are both kept.
position_hint: Middle of the group, among the films on the occasions of wanting: after the films on what wanting takes its object to be and on the conditions that sharpen it, before the films on particular takings. Its single day, empty to full, is a natural hinge, and it is the group's only film in which a crowd is the whole subject and nobody in it is shown.
risks: Drifting into a sunset postcard with history read over it: the sea sunset is the payoff only because it is where the fast time stops, and the stone carries the argument at both ends.

Presenting anyone on the lawn as wanting: the high frame is chosen so that nobody is identifiable, and the voice says in terms that it does not know why anyone is there. No ground-level shot shows a face.
Children: the stone's words name them and kites draw them; no child is framed, followed or recognisable at any point.

The lawn's recent political history, including its occupation in 2022, is out of the film entirely: no banner, no site, no reference in voice or caption, and the frame looks away from the administrative buildings at the lawn's northern end.

The reclamation and development at the lawn's north-western edge is a live land and planning dispute; it is kept out of frame and out of the voice, and the 1892 argument about sand removal and the sea wall is left in the research record for the same reason.
Calling the walk's exempt branch 'wholesome': the source says only 'not unwholesome', and only the kindly feeding of animals is called wholesome outright.
Adopting the French traveller's accusation as the film's own: 'pretext' is quoted as his word and set against the stone's claim; the film rules on neither.

Using the 1907 history's anecdote of a jockey who 'fell down dead' after selling races: it reads as kamma-as-fate and its own author doubts it, so the whole of that informant's passage is left out, not only the ending.
Naming the 1872 scheme's participants: the source calls them only 'a few sparks' and the film keeps them anonymous.
A state parade or its rehearsals occupying the lawn on the shooting day, which would also bring a military register the film does not want.
drop_if: No high vantage at the landward end can be obtained for a full day, since the film is built on one fixed frame.
The lawn cannot be filmed on an ordinary day without political material, a state event or security restrictions in frame.
The inscribed stone no longer stands at the sea wall, or cannot be filmed, in which case the film has no statement of aim to open and close on.
The owner or manager of the lawn refuses filming, or requires the crowd to be staged or cleared.

connections.note: A cold upland plain turned into a sanatorium on the belief that weather and a sound body change how a person moves, filmed at ground level at dawn as frost melts on one blade of grass. That film deliberately left out racing, the season and promenading to keep the two films apart. Both touch the colonial belief in air as health; that film is about the conditions that sharpen wanting, this one about its aims, and the cinema is opposite: one blade in real time against a whole crowd in fast time.

A king's throne in a museum a few kilometres away, filmed at night as a stepped approach across a dark room to a single object. That film uses C005's guarding-with-usefulness exemption on one object; this one uses the same line on one piece of open ground and on a crowd. Interior, night, one lamp and one object against exterior, one whole day and thousands of people. Together they take the district to five films.

Proposed in the blind GRP-02 selection as a kraal site and an elephant nursery where the same gesture, a bottle of milk held to a calf, is made for two aims seventy years apart. Both are C005's 'the why, not the what'; that film sets two aims against each other across two places and pays off on a cut from an archival photograph, this one keeps one place and one frame and pays off on a change of speed, not a cut.

selection.reason: Rebuilt from scratch on 2026-09-26 on the blind GRP-02 selection's proposal, which was tested against the nineteenth-century sources and kept with corrections: the walk's dates and wording as the proposal gave them are a modern conflation, and the racing and 'field of fire' claims rest on secondary sources. What survives is stronger than the proposal: a public walk whose aim was cut into a stone at its edge and then contradicted, in print, by the next witnesses, which is C005's question asked by documents. Its weakness is that it is a city lawn whose frames depend on a crowd, a sunset and a vantage that has not been secured.

review.note: This record's body was replaced in full on 2026-09-26 in the blind GRP-02 re-selection; nothing of the previous version was read or kept except the fixed fields and the old title, now in aliases. The previous status was already pending, so no confirmation or rejection has been reset, but under standing decision 9 any earlier reading of this record no longer applies. The concepts are unchanged (C005 primary, C006 supporting). The location, proposed by Claude, is the open seafront lawn in front of the old fort of the capital, raced on until 1893 and given a promenade along its sea wall by Governor Sir Henry Ward in 1856-1859, at whose sea edge a stone post records that the walk was recommended to his successors in the interest of the ladies and children of the town. The film is one real day as a locked time-lapse from a high vantage at the landward end, cut with real-time ground shots of the stone at dawn and at night; the payoff is the moment the time-lapse slows into real time as the sun touches the sea over the full lawn. The title has changed to follow the film. What to judge: first, whether a city lawn with a sunset and a crowd meets the footage-led standard (the record argues that the daily transformation seen from one fixed height is the frame, and that it is the group's only crowd film); second, whether a full-day high vantage and the managing authority's permission are obtainable; third, whether the district can take a fifth film (the district goes from 4 to 5 with this one). Corrections to the proposal: the stone says the walk was commenced in 1856 and completed in 1859, not 'completed in 1856' as the widely repeated modern quotation has it; one 1882 transcription gives the words as 'for the use of the ladies and gentlemen', and both versions are kept; the 'field of fire' origin and the 1820s start of racing could not be confirmed from any primary and are out of the voice; and the date 1853 given in a 1938 memoir is impossible, since Ward took up the government on 11 May 1855.

suggested_location.name: Galle Face Green and the Galle Face Walk, with the Ward inscription stone at the sea wall, Colombo

suggested_location.region: Colombo District, Western Province: the seafront between Colombo Fort (Colombo 01) and Kollupitiya (Colombo 03) (verified by reverse geocoding the coordinates to Colombo District; no boundary ambiguity)
suggested_location.why_here: It is the one place found on the island where the aim of a public work was cut into the work itself and then contradicted in print by the next people to write about it. The stone at the sea wall states that the walk was 'recommended to his successors in the interest of the ladies and children'; a newspaper editor gave a practical reason (the red laterite dust spoiled boots and clothing); a French traveller of 1864 saw neither ladies nor children there and called the cleared ground a pretext for a passion for turf; a racing club used it for decades and left because it could not fence it. That is C005's question, whether the same act is wanting depends on an aim the act does not show, asked by documents rather than read into a place. And the place films: a long flat lawn lying along the sea wall, the sun setting into open ocean beside it, and a daily transformation from an empty plane at dawn to thousands of people and hundreds of kites at dusk, which from one high fixed point is a single frame that fills like a tide and in which nobody can be identified.

historical_thread.story: The lawn is the open ground that lay south of the fort of Colombo, between the sea and the lake. How and when it was first cleared is not documented in any primary reached: C. Brooke Elliott, a lawyer writing his memoir The Real Ceylon in 1938, says it 'was originally the glacis levelled by the military authorities, so that the guns of the Fort could sweep the open ground to the South', and Twentieth Century Impressions of Ceylon (1907) calls it 'the fine open military reservation bearing the world-famed name of the Galle Face'. Horse racing was held on it for most of the nineteenth century: François Devay, a French traveller who was in Colombo in 1864 (Journal d'un voyage dans l'Inde anglaise... en 1864, Paris 1867, vol. II, pp. 213-214), describes the English as having 'stripped a whole vast space, south of the fort, under the pretext of green lawns and a racecourse' ('sous prétexte de pelouses vertes et de champ de courses'), carrying 'the fiftieth degree of latitude' to the ninth out of 'la passion du turf et du gazon vert'. Governor Sir Henry George Ward, who took up the government on 11 May 1855 (A. M. Ferguson, quoted in J. P. Lewis, List of Inscriptions on Tombstones and Monuments in Ceylon, 1913), built a sea wall and a promenade along the sea edge of the lawn. Devay walked it at dawn and before sunset and describes a long straight sanded walk 'with a few benches', held up by a retaining wall about two metres above the sand, with the monsoon surf throwing spray over the lawns beyond the road; the walk, he writes, 'was begun in 1856 by Sir Henry Ward, finished in 1859, and, as an inscription cut on a post of grey marble expresses it, recommanded to his successors, in the interest of the ladies and children of Colombo'. He adds: 'I do not know whether at this time of year the walk is thought bad for the health; but I never saw there either ladies or children profiting from the solicitude of Sir Henry Ward and his successors, and yet I was always there at the only hours when this promenade can be used pleasantly or with impunity, early in the morning or in the evening a little before sunset.' A. M. Ferguson, editor of the Ceylon Observer, writing of Ward's governorship (quoted by Lewis, 1913), gives the reason as practical: 'Before its construction a walk on the seaside of our beautiful and healthy esplanade was next to impossible for ladies in consequence of the effects of the red cabook or laterite dust on boots and clothing.' John Ferguson, recalling his arrival in November 1861 (Ceylon in 1903), calls the lawn 'the maidan of Colombo, where all Society of an afternoon "eat the air"'. Twentieth Century Impressions (1907) calls the walk 'the Corso of Colombo', where the principal residents drove up and down in carriages every afternoon, and the lawn a 'lung' for the city. The racing on the lawn is described in the same volume. A planter's recollection printed there calls the course 'a nasty course... hard in dry weather and sometimes very heavy going in wet'. The sporting journalist F. D. Mitchell, who arrived in 1872, is quoted on the crisis of that year: 'A few sparks were anxious to ramp the public by pulling old Cyclops for one race in the hope of winning another; but the sparks got ramped and there was a general break up of the Club. There had been a thorough good gamble this year...'; for 1873 and 1874 no jockeys were allowed. The club needed 'a course that it could fence in, and from which it could exclude the ordinary traffic, which it frequently failed to do on the Galle Face, for we read of such curious accidents as a cart containing beer barrels being run into by the field in an actual race'; the races moved to the new course in Cinnamon Gardens, opened on 22 June 1893. The walk's sea wall partly collapsed in 1892; the Municipal Council blamed the Government's removal of 80,000 to 90,000 tons of sand a year from the beach for the harbour reclamation works, and the Director of Public Works, R. K. MacBride, blamed the wall's cabook superstructure (Ceylon Administration Reports for 1892). Golf, rugby and cricket were also played on the lawn in the 1870s to 1890s according to modern accounts, and in the twentieth century it became the city's main open public space, managed since 2014 by the Sri Lanka Ports Authority. A stone carrying the inscription stands at the sea edge of the promenade today; travel guides by Royston Ellis (1992 onward) say the original stone is in the old Town Hall museum in Pettah.
historical_thread.how_it_binds: C005 draws its line by aim, not by act: the same earning, spending, dressing and eating are greed-rooted when done for taste, beauty, display or amusement and not unwholesome when faith, kindness, compassion or wisdom 'considering usefulness' stands in front [C005-M:L9] [C005-M:L11] [C005-M:L13] [C005-M:L15–L19], and its list of occasions includes gambling, sport and watching sport [C005-M:L5] and pleasure trips [C005-M:L7]. This lawn's record is a sequence of stated aims for one act, keeping ground open and walking on it, and the aims are of exactly the kinds the Margaya sorts: benefit to others (the stone), protection of clothing (Ferguson's dust), pleasure in turf (Devay's charge), sport and betting (the racing years). The documents also disagree with each other, and the one statement of aim carved on the site survives in two wordings. That is not a reading the film brings to the place; it is what the record is. C006 adds the weights: strong for courses of action such as taking what is not given, weak for ordinary fondness; heavier with a justifying view, heavier unprompted, heavier when flat [C006-M:L19]. The 1872 record of a scheme to take the betting public's money, set beside the ordinary pleasures of race days, is the strong-weak distinction as a document. The film uses both concepts to show what the camera and the documents cannot reach: the aim and the dials belong to single minds, and the texts say so.
what_is_certain: The inscription existed by 1864 and dated the walk: François Devay (1867, vol. II, p. 213) says the walk was begun in 1856 by Sir Henry Ward and finished in 1859, 'as an inscription cut on a post of grey marble expresses it', and quotes it as 'recommanded to his successors, in the interest of the ladies and children of Colombo'. Twentieth Century Impressions of Ceylon (1907, Colombo chapter) gives the same dates and 'in the interests of the ladies and children of Colombo'; John Ferguson (Ceylon in 1903) and A. M. Ferguson as quoted by Lewis (1913) give the same wording without the dates.
Ward took up the government of Ceylon on 11 May 1855 and left on 30 June 1860 (A. M. Ferguson, Ceylon in 1847-1860, quoted by Lewis, 1913).

A. M. Ferguson gave the walk's purpose as practical: before it, a walk on the seaside of the esplanade 'was next to impossible for ladies in consequence of the effects of the red cabook or laterite dust on boots and clothing' (quoted by Lewis, 1913).

Devay, walking there at dawn and before sunset in 1864, 'never saw there either ladies or children', and described the cleared lawn as made 'under the pretext of green lawns and a racecourse' out of 'the passion for turf and green grass' (1867, vol. II, pp. 213-214, author's translation from the French).

Horse racing was held on the lawn in 1864 (Devay) and until 1893, when the Turf Club moved to the new course in Cinnamon Gardens, opened on 22 June 1893, because it wanted a course it could fence and from which it could exclude the ordinary traffic (Twentieth Century Impressions of Ceylon, 1907, racing chapter).

The 1872 racing crisis as F. D. Mitchell described it: a scheme 'to ramp the public by pulling old Cyclops for one race in the hope of winning another', which failed ('the sparks got ramped'), and 'a general break up of the Club'; no jockeys were allowed in 1873 and 1874 (quoted in Twentieth Century Impressions of Ceylon, 1907).

The walk's sea wall partly collapsed in 1892, and its cause was disputed in print between the Municipal Council (sand removal) and the Director of Public Works (the cabook superstructure) (Ceylon Administration Reports for 1892).
The site lies in Colombo District (reverse geocoding of the coordinates; OpenStreetMap).
what_is_disputed: The inscription's wording. Devay (1864), Ferguson (1903), Twentieth Century Impressions (1907) and Lewis (1913) give 'in the interest(s) of the ladies and children of Colombo'; the Handbook of the Bengal Presidency (1882) transcribes the stone line by line as 'Galle Face Walk. Commenced By Sir Henry Ward, In 1856; Completed 1859, And recommended to his Successors for the use of The Ladies and Gentlemen.' The majority reading is probably right and the 1882 reading a copying error, but both are kept and neither is averaged.

The walk's dates. The stone as transcribed in 1864, 1882 and 1907 says commenced 1856, completed 1859. The widely repeated modern quotation 'Galle Face Walk completed in 1856 and recommended to his successors...' (Wikipedia and many travel pages, with no source) conflates the two dates and matches no nineteenth-century transcription. Elliott (1938) gives 1853, which is impossible: Ward did not arrive until May 1855. Some modern accounts give 1859 as the date the promenade was 'laid out'.

Whether the stone now on site is the original. Ellis (Sri Lanka by Rail, 1992, and later Bradt guides) says the original is in the old Town Hall museum in Pettah; recent accounts describe a stone at the sea edge. Could not confirm which stone stands there, or whether it stands where Devay's 'post of grey marble' stood ('about the middle of the Promenade, near the sea', 1882).

When racing began on the lawn. Modern accounts give the early 1820s under Governor Barnes and a first recorded meet in 1821; the planter M. H. Thomas, writing for the 1907 volume, says racing 'has been an annual institution in Ceylon from some time in the forties' and that there are no written records of the earliest days. The earliest primary reached that places a racecourse on this lawn is Devay (1864).

The lawn's first clearing. Elliott (1938) says it was levelled as a glacis for the fort's guns; one modern web account says the Dutch used it to aim cannon at the Portuguese, which cannot be right as stated and has no source. Could not confirm from any primary who cleared it or when; it is out of the voice.

The name. Modern accounts derive it from a Dutch or Portuguese word for the front of the fort facing Galle, or from a Sinhala name for the rocky shore ('Gal Bokka'); Brohier (1965) cites Tennent on it. Not examined further and not used.

what_to_film: The spine: one locked time-lapse from a single high vantage above the landward (north-eastern) end of the lawn, looking south-west down its length to the sea wall, the sea horizon and the old hotel at the far end, from about 05:00 to full dark on one day. Interval long enough that people register only as moving points; exposure ramped through sunrise and sunset. No zoom, no pan, no motion control.

The payoff: at the moment the sun touches the sea, the time-lapse is slowed progressively (interval shortened on the day, not in post) until it is real time, and the full lawn is held live with synced sound for several minutes as the light goes.

Two real-time ground sequences at the inscription stone at the sea edge of the promenade: before dawn in blue light with surf behind, and after dark under the nearest street lamp with the lit crowd defocused behind it. Macro across the carved lines, never lingering on the walk's name.
Sound: sea and surf recorded at the wall through the whole day; the crowd's rising murmur recorded from the edge of the lawn in the afternoon and evening, never close to any group; no music.

Framing discipline: the high frame excludes the administrative buildings at the lawn's northern end and the reclaimed land to the north-west; no ground shot shows a face, a child, a vendor or a stall.
Not filmed: any drone shot (the area around the fort is restricted); any banner, political gathering or state ceremony; any archival photograph (the group's archive cut belongs to another film).
suggested_location.access: A public open space, open day and night. Management passed from the Urban Development Authority to the Sri Lanka Ports Authority in 2014 and has been carried out since 2016 by Sri Lanka Port Management and Consultancy Services (per the Wikipedia article); filming permission for a crew and tripod on the promenade would be sought from them, and police and security clearance is likely to be needed because of the government buildings at the northern end. The high vantage is the hard part: it needs a full day on a roof or high floor of a building at the landward end of the lawn looking south-west down it (the towers at its north-eastern corner are the obvious candidates), with the owner's permission, power and a secured camera for about fifteen hours. None of this has been sought. No drone is used.
suggested_location.best_time: A clear, dry-season weekend day, most likely between December and March, when the evening crowd is largest and sunsets over the sea are clearest; the south-west monsoon (roughly May to September) gives heavier surf over the wall but more cloud and rain. Avoid the weeks around 4 February, when the lawn has been used for the national day parade and its rehearsals, and any public holiday or political event; the shooting day must be an ordinary one. One day from about 04:30 set-up to 20:00.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only, 2026-09-26. Read in the printed texts on the Internet Archive: Devay (1867, vol. II, pp. 213-214, in French; translations in this record are mine), the Handbook of the Bengal Presidency (1882, Ceylon section, the line-by-line transcription of the stone), Lewis's List of Inscriptions (1913, entry 1276, quoting A. M. Ferguson's Ceylon in 1847-1860 on Ward), John Ferguson's Ceylon in 1903 (the 1861 recollection), Twentieth Century Impressions of Ceylon (1907: the Colombo chapter on the walk and the racing chapter with Thomas's and Mitchell's recollections and the 1893 move), Elliott's The Real Ceylon (1938) and the Ceylon Administration Reports for 1892 (the sea-wall collapse). Reached only through full-text search snippets: Ellis (1992 and later) on the original stone being in the old Town Hall museum. The proposal's key quotation ('completed in 1856') was tested and fails: every nineteenth-century transcription reached gives commenced 1856, completed 1859; the modern quotation is repeated on dozens of pages with no source (failure mode 3). The 1882 transcription's 'ladies and gentlemen' is a genuine variant and is kept. Elliott's 1853 is impossible on its own terms (failure mode 5). The 'field of fire' origin and the 1821 start of racing were not found in any primary (failure modes 3 and 6: the silence of the primaries is not a denial, and both stay in what_is_disputed). The 1907 racing chapter was taken whole where used: the same page's informant tells of a jockey who 'fell down dead' after selling races, which reads as kamma-as-fate and which the author himself calls possibly bazaar gossip, so that informant's passage is excluded entirely (failure mode 8). Deliberately not entered: the 2022 occupation of the lawn (the 'GotaGoGama' protest site, a live political episode) and the Port City reclamation to the north-west (a live land and development dispute); the 1892 sand-removal argument is kept in the thread as history but out of the voice because of its resonance with the latter. District verified by reverse geocoding (Colombo District, Western Province). District budget: Colombo was at 3 films outside GRP-02/03; IDEA-0014 (written this round) took it to 4 and this film takes it to 5, above the preferred 4 and below the closed 7; the GRP-03 Colombo proposal (IDEA-0037) was refused, so the count stands at 5. Images: all five files confirmed to exist by imageinfo query on 2026-09-26; the only Commons photograph of the inscription stone (1988) has an identifiable child leaning on it and is deliberately not carried. The strongest objection is the footage half of the test: this is a flat city lawn, and its best frame, a sunset over the sea with a crowd and kites, is close to a postcard; the case for it is that the fixed-height day, empty to full, is a genuinely unusual frame and the only way to film a crowd without anyone in it being shown, but the reviewer should weigh that. Access to a high vantage for a full day, the managing authority's permission, security clearance and the stone's present state are all unverified.

unknowns: Whether a building owner at the landward end of the lawn will allow a camera on a roof or high floor for a full day, and whether its view down the lawn excludes the government buildings and the reclaimed land.
Whether the lawn's managing authority and the police will permit a crew and tripods on the promenade from before dawn to after dark.
Whether the stone now at the sea wall is the original or a copy, and exactly where it stands; its present wording has not been seen.
The primary evidence for when racing began on the lawn and for the 'field of fire' origin, neither found.
Ellis's statement that the original stone is in the old Town Hall museum was read only in a search snippet.
Whether any national event, parade rehearsal or political gathering will occupy the lawn on a chosen date.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location was proposed by Claude and awaits Chathura's review; it has not been confirmed. The inscription's wording and dates, Devay's observations, the Fergusons' statements, the racing history and the 1892 sea-wall dispute are documentary and were read in printed nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century texts; the location of the original stone is from a modern guidebook read only in a snippet; the lawn's present appearance is from photographs; access, permission and filming conditions are desk research and unverified. No scene or shot has been filmed.
